speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter which deeply concerns me. In light of the fact that Soviet dissident, Anatoly Shcharansky, is currently being force-fed to end his hunger strike over the legitimate complaint that he is no longer allowed to receive mail or visits from relatives, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Cariboo-Chilcotin (Mr. Greenaway):
That this Government condemn the actions of the Soviets in the case of Anatoly Shcharansky, and that it urge that steps be taken to put an immediate end to this flagrant violation of human rights, which is in direct contravention of the Helsinki Accord.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
maintopic: MOTIONS UNDER S.O. 43   HUMAN RIGHTS CONDEMNATION OF TREATMENT OF ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY BY SOVIET AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the case raised by my colleague is one of the most tragic violations of human rights the world has seen. Anatoly Shcharansky, a computer scientist, has been imprisoned in the Soviet Union because of his desire to leave that country. He has asked for simple release from the Soviet Union to rejoin his family.
In the light of this motion, and as we have a Canadian delegation in Moscow at the present time, a delegation which is seeking to restore scientific exchanges between Canada and the U.S.S.R., I would make a plea that one of the basic things this delegation can do is to bring the case of Anatoly Shcharansky before the Soviet authorities, that they make these exchanges conditional upon the release of Anatoly Shcharansky before any are carried out. I would extend that plea further to include the Andrei Sakharovs of this world and to the many other scientists, people of international repute, who are being held in prison in the Soviet Union.

maintopic: MOTIONS UNDER S.O. 43   HUMAN RIGHTS CONDEMNATION OF TREATMENT OF ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY BY SOVIET AUTHORITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, very briefly, I want to join with the mover and the seconder of the motion in urging Soviet officials and representatives of the Government of Canada to meet to discuss the problem of
refusniks in Russia in general and, in particular, the specific problem of Anatoly Shcharansky. I think it is quite clear to everyone that the lack of human rights within the Soviet Union is a matter of grave concern.
In the attempt by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to establish a more cordial and better relationship with the Government of Russia, one of the things that ought to be considered is the human rights record of the Soviet Union. Pressure must be brought to bear to bring about the release of people who would like to leave the Soviet Union, and who, under the Soviet Constitution, legally should be able to leave but who are suffering as a result of their attempt to exercise that freedom.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (External Relations)):
maintopic: MOTIONS UNDER S.O. 43   HUMAN RIGHTS CONDEMNATION OF TREATMENT OF ANATOLY SHCHARANSKY BY SOVIET AUTHORITIES
speechtext: We support this motion because as so many Canadians-I would even say the vast majority of Canadians-We are very concerned about this fundamental negation of the most elementary human rights in the case of Anatoly Shcharansky. Madam Speaker, as you know, the Government of Canada has interceded on behalf of Mr. Shcharansky several times in recent years, including our intervention at the Madrid Conference on European Security and Co-operation. More recently, that is, on October 22, we informed the Embassy of the U.S.S.R. in Canada of our strong opposition to this intolerable negation of human rights in the case of Anatoly Shcharansky. I therefore join my colleague from Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and the House Leader for the New Democratic Party (Mr. Deans) in asking that the Soviet Union allow Anatoly Shcharansky to leave and also to receive visits from members of his family.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader

Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), and myself, had the opportunity to go to the Soviet Union to speak to a number of Soviet officials in order to impress upon them the importance that Canadians attach to this issue. I think the message we want the Soviet officials to understand is that we look forward to the possibility of an improved climate in East-West relations, but in order to do this, this is

one issue that must be addressed and is one about which we, as parliamentarians, feel very strongly.

subsubtopic: EL SALVADOR-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF INTERNATIONAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a tragic civil war continues in El Salvador, with assassinations, disappearances and murders. Last week, El Salvadoran Church officials reported 4,400 documented cases of victims of this violence in the first ten months of 1982. Bishop Arturo Rivera Y Damas and El Salvadoran Protestant Church leaders have called for a dialogue on how the reign of terror might be ended and urgent attention given to the needs of nearly one million refugees, mostly women and children. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That the Government of Canada join with concerned regional Governments, such as Mexico and Venezuela, and international humanitarian institutions, in establishing an international commission to consult with all parties in the conflict. This commission would report to the Secretary General of the United Nations with practical procedures for a dialogue to end the war and measures to address the deep social and economic problems of El Salvador.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO ASSIST PRIVATE SECTOR IN CREATION OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Economic Development, who knows only too well that 539,000 jobs,
289,000	in the manufacturing sector alone, have been lost in this country since August last year. In view of the fact that the Minister has been in office with his new portfolios for almost seven weeks now, would he tell the House what new steps he has taken to ensure that the private sector, once again, will start creating jobs instead of cutting employment which is falling so heavily on all Canadians, but especially on the youth of this land, where we find, nationally, that 20 per cent of the youth are out of work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not know where the Hon. Member for York-Peel has been. There have been a series of announcements by the Government on a regular basis. Perhaps one of the most significant, in terms of direct job creation, was the NEED Program announced by the Minister of Employment and Immigration just a short time ago.
Oral Questions
I do not think this is the time and place for me to recite at length all the Programs, whether they be in the research and development sector or whether they be in the industrial development sector under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, concerning the regional efforts which have been made. I will be quite happy to take the time of the House to go through all these matters if the House wishes, and call upon the Ministers of each Department, on this side of the House, to explain in more detail some of the specific initiatives which have been taken, but the whole thrust of economic development under this Government has been to provide job-creation, but job-creation in areas which will be of long term benefit to the economy of the country and not simply direct job-creation which does not make that contribution. That has been the thrust, is the thrust now, and will continue to be the thrust.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Minister of State for Economic Development, who must know, notwithstanding the efforts his Government may have made, that the unemployment figure is up by 500,000 today compared to only last year. Would the Minister specifically indicate if he has given any consideration to encouraging or stimulating the pension funds of this country, in the private or public sector, by putting more equity money into business in order to help create some of these jobs that are being lost at the present time? If he has given some consideration to this approach, would he indicate to the House what the response from the pension fund people has been?

Madam Speaker, I think the Hon. Member knows full well that the pension fund investments in this country comprise, of course, one of the greatest sources of capital in equity markets. The Hon. Member may be referring to the fact that the pension funds are limited by legislation with respect to the kind of investments they can make, that is to say, that pension funds are limited to a specific purpose, to provide security for people who are retired from the work force. The pension legislation, whether at the provincial or federal level, tries to balance the security issue of pension investments with that part of the fund which may be used for other purposes, more specifically, funds going to companies in certain sectors which do not have an earnings record, a dividend payment record which would justify, if you like, investment for pension purposes per se, but that matter has been considered for many years.
If the Hon. Member has specific representations to make with respect to whether the present amount designated provincially or federally is inadequate for investments other than those that are stipulated in the legislation in question in each province, and federally, then I suggest that he put those

November 19, 1982
Oral Questions

I think it is an area worth considering, but I do think it is very important that that balance be maintained. That balance was established with very specific purposes in mind.

Again I direct a question to the Minister of State for Economic Development, who will recall a "Government and Business" personal perspective that he wrote in March of this year, which was circulated at the Liberal convention. In the perspective, or viewpoint, the Minister stated:
I do not recall a period when the relationships between Government and business were as poor as they are today.
Would the Minister indicate what steps he has taken to improve those relationships and, specifically, how does he reconcile the $200 million that is being asked for in the form of equity in Canadair, when he stated in the same paper on page 5, referring to Canadair:
When we do not have sufficient public capital available to satisfy pressing social needs ... it is painful to see scarce capital deployed in a manufacturing concern best left to private enterprise.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF TAXES ON ALBERTA PETROCHEMICAL COMPANY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question, too, is directed to the Minister of State for Economic Development. One of the sectors which could provide the longterm jobs which the Minister is referring to is the petrochemical industry which has been crippled as a result of the heavy, up-front taxes imposed under the National Energy Program. One of those companies is Alberta Gas Chemicals Limited which has stated the Company can survive the world-wide recession and the legislated increases in the price of natural gas, but not both of these plus the federal Government taxes on natural gas. This is a wholly owned Canadian company which employs some 170 people and exports about 85 per cent of its product to the international marketplace. Because of the heavy taxes imposed by the federal Government, the Company has been forced into a position to join with a New Zealand company in a joint venture to develop a new methanol plant in New Zealand. Is the Minister aware of this, and what steps is he taking to avert that transition?

Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and
Resources): Madam Speaker, as my colleague, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, told the Hon. Member this week, we are having internal discussions at this time. At the same time we have to compete in the world market, and there is a squeeze in the petrochemical world market at this time. That is a very important factor.

Madam Speaker, I am almost as unhappy about what happened at Charlottetown before I became the Minister and since, as is my hon. friend. The design works on the air terminal are some six or seven months late now. If everything goes well-and I hope it will-tenders will be called in the fall of 1983. In case my hon. friends are interested in knowing why this has taken place, I might say that one of the rules of the implementation of the democratic process in the Department of Transport is that, before going on with the construction of air terminal, we ask the carriers if they would look at and agree to the costs which will be incurred by them as renters of the terminal. It is quite easy to imagine that those costs are always too high in the carrier's view. Thus we are lead to prolonged negotiation and delays. This was one of the reasons for delays at the Charlottetown airport. Finally, conclusions have been reached in discussions on rentals with the carriers, and this is why we can move now. subsubtopic: MR. KING-IMPOSITION OF METRIC SYSTEM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my duty and privilege to present a petition to this House on behalf of 3,140 citizens of Okanagan-Similkameen, British Columbia. An attached letter over the signature of Lelannd Haver of Westbank, B.C., states in part:
We the members of "Metric Won't Do" wish to bring to your attention a matter of paramount importance at this time, that being the whole question of metrication-
The nature of the petition is to pray and beseech this House to re-evaluate the Government's decision to implement metric and stop the onslaught of worthless and excessive expenditures for a measurement that is less than perfect, with due respect for truth and freedom of choice.
The petitioners hope, Madam Speaker, that you will find their petition in order and that through their efforts, with the co-operation of the Members of this House, the citizens of Canada may be spared the further imposition of forced metric and the forced abandonment of Imperial measure, which they say was established from practical and spiri'ual origins.

subsubtopic: MR. LEWYCKY-SCLATER, MAN.-CALL FOR RESTORATION OF POSTAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the Member of Parliament for Dauphin, Manitoba, it is my duty to present before this House a petition representing residents of Sclater, Manitoba and its surrounding community.
The postal services of Sclater were, and remain, withdrawn following the destruction by fire of the postal facilities there. Given the fact that the former post office was located in a general store and, as such, constituted an important focal point of the community, and that residents must now travel in excess of 50 kilometres in order to obtain their mail, the petitioners therefore request that this House ask the Minister responsible for Canada Post Corporation to instruct the President and Chief Executive Officer to restore in full the postal facilities and services formerly enjoyed by the community of Sclater, Manitoba.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (President of Treasury Board) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
that Bill C-119, An Act to repeal certain Statutes that have ceased to be in force or have become unnecessary, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to move second reading of Bill C-119, the miscellaneous statutes repeal Bill. This Bill, together with Bill C-118, the records retention amendment Bill, which was enacted earlier this session, forms an important legislative component of the Government's current regulatory reform program.
[ Translation]
This program was launched by the Federal Government in the fall of 1980, in response to rising concern in the private sector and among consumers about the potential effects of unnecessary or obsolete regualtions on Canadians. Hon. Members may recall that in the fall of 1979, at the First Ministers' Conference on the Economy, these problems were discussed at length, and it was agreed that the Economic Council of Canada would be asked to give careful scrutiny to the regulatory process in Canada. The Council made a thorough study of the subject and submitted a preliminary report in November 1979, followed by its final report in July 1981. In the meantime, Members of the Senate and the House of Commons also made a careful study of these issues. Hon. Members are aware of the excellent work done by the Standing Joint Committee on Regulatory and Other Statutory Instruments. In July 1980, the Committee presented a major report on various aspects of the regulatory process and of parliamentary reform. A special committee of the House had been established to study regulatory reform, and it too submitted a report, in December of the same year.
The Government's regulatory reform program, of which this Bill is a component, is directly responsive not only to the concerns expressed but also to the recommendations for reform that have been made by all the various groups and participants from both Parliament and private sector. The program reflects a growing awareness that there can be unintended negative effects on the efficiency of Government and industry resulting
from the way regulations are implemented and administered. Therefore, the Government must make every effort to ensure both that the objectives of Government regulations are met as efficiently as possible and that unnecessary costs or other negative effects associated with regulations are reduced to a minimum.
The Government will then assess the progress that has been made and consider proposals with a view to taking further measures in the future. In establishing its regulatory reform program, the Government had two major objectives in mind: to improve public administration by reforming the federal regulatory process and to remove undue regulatory pressures on the Canadian economy.
The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) entrusted co-ordination of the program to the President of the Treasury Board.
I want to recognize the very good work of my distinguished predecessor, the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), in this very key area of regulatory reform. Our approach to reform is essentially one of improving the management of the federal regulatory process. We will strive to manage the regulatory process in such a way that the proposed regulation is scrutinized to ensure that it is effective. Existing regulations will be reviewed and assessed to ensure that it still meets their goals at acceptable cost.
We believe that the existing regulatory activities of Government, particularly in the area of economic regulations, should be reassessed to ensure that they are consistent with the Government's economic and social policy objectives. We believe that the continuing flow of new regulatory proposals should be subject to an analysis of the potential impacts.
Before being asked to make decisions, Ministers must be provided with better information on the cost and benefits of regulatory proposals, on alternatives to regulatory intervention, on the effects that the proposals might have on the distribution of wealth and income. We believe that there is room for further improvement in the federal regulatory process and its administration. This process and administration should ensure more effective consultation with the private sector during the various steps and stages of regulatory decisionmaking, as well as an improvement where necessary of the accountability of federal regulators.
Our continuing regulatory reform program encompasses a variety of projects, each aimed at furthering the underlying objectives established by the Government. The Bill before us is the product of one of these projects which called on federal regulatory departments to review their statutes and regulations and to weed out obsolete, unnecessary or duplicative provisions.



November 19, 1982



The Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act would provide for repeal of the 124 acts which have been found to be obsolete to date. Many of these acts have not been enforced for some time, and most are not concerned with regulation. This bill is basically a housekeeping measure, and its main concern is with the primary objective of the regulatory reform program, which is to improve public administration. In fact, it is the initial result, when we speak of repeal legislation, of a very wide-ranging study carried out by federal ministers with a view to ridding our legislation of all unnecessary elements and updating it as much as possible.

To sum up, this miscellaneous statute reform Bill is an integral part of the Government's over-all regulatory reform program and represents an important first step in tackling the job of legislative housekeeping. 1 believe it represents an important measure, among several, that we are pursuing to improve public administration and over-all management of federal regulations. I believe that the introduction of the bill and the cosideration now being given to it by Parliament should give an important message to both the public and private sectors. Members of Parliament through the Special Committee on Regulatory Reform and through the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments have stressed the need for a concerted effort toward regulatory reform. This Government is in agreement that reform is needed. We are committed to take action through our regulatory reform program.
We cannot do everything at one time. Some of our objectives may be difficult to achieve. However, no one should make the mistake that our commitment is in doubt because we may not be tackling a particular problem at a particular point in time or because it is taking some time to see change. We do have a strong commitment to regulatory reform. Our commitment should be judged on the basis of whether we deliver the reforms that are identified as targets in our work program. We promise to weed out obsolete, unnecessary and unenforceable federal statutes. We are delivering on that promise by presenting this Bill before Parliament.
I want to repeat that it represents some very important work done by my distinguished predecessor as President of the Treasury Board, who is now Minister of State for Economic Development.
In its recent submission to the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, the Canadian Bar Association commented that Parliament had not done well in handling certain types of legislation. They commented on our inability to deal effectively and quickly with routine bills that did not involve contentious policy issues and that should not give rise to partisan differences.
1 hope that Members of the House will all agree that this Bill before us now should be viewed as such an item and that collectively we will be able to give it prompt attention. For our part, the Government will be providing to Members who examine the Bill in Committee stage a copy of a discussion
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
paper which sets out a brief justification for proceeding with the repeal of each of the 124 statutes listed.
Therefore, I ask Hon. Members of all Parties to support this Bill, and consistent with Parliament's responsibility to carefully scrutinize legislation, to enact the Bill as expeditiously as possible. By doing so, Parliament will be reaffirming its interests in, and commitment to, regulatory reform. It is a message that I think Parliament should send to the Canadian public.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the House to note that this is the first piece of legislation which has been introduced by the Hon. Minister in his renewed capacity as President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray). Therefore, it is the first opportunity that I have had, at least in this function, to express my good wishes to him in the fulfillment of the responsibility of his portfolio. I also note that the Hon. Member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang), who was in the House and will be back shortly, is the new Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board.
This means that with respect to the business of regulatory reform, the repeal of miscellaneous statutes, and items such as Bill C-133 with respect to the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act, we have two completely new and uncluttered minds to direct to these problems. 1 know that this will be of some importance to you, Mr. Speaker, and to other Hon. Members in the House of Commons as we consider these problems. I sincerely say to the Minister, through Your Honour, that I wish him well. The process is a good one and we should consider the statutes from time to time.
The full process of regulatory reform is important to the country. I think Hon. Members would be interested in knowing that there are 11 statutes from the Department of Agriculture, one from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, five from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, three from the Department of the Environment, 11 from the Department of Finance, four from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, three from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, two from the Department of Insurance, 11 from the Department of Labour, two from the Department of National Health and Welfare, three from the Department of National Revenue, three from the Department of Public Works, four from the Department of the Secretary of State, one from the Department of Supply and Services, 59 from the Department of Transport and one from the Department of Veterans Affairs.
The list of bills is there. Therefore, I am pleased to hear the hon. gentleman say that he will supply the members of the Committee with a discussion paper and it will be a large one, I imagine, with respect to all those Bills, and it will be of immense help to the Committee.
From the point of view of the Official Opposition, I want to say to the Minister that it is our intention to expedite this matter. Certainly, we must do other things to reform the

November 19, 1982
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
regulatory system. We must take a critical look at the institution of the Comptroller Genera! to see where it can be strengthened. The late Robert Andras was the President of the Treasury Board who finally brought the Bill involving the Comptroller General before the House of Commons. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that the distinguished gentleman consulted and presented that Bill so well the matter went through very quickly. He was moved to take decision to Cabinet which ultimately approved it as a result of the work of the Hon. Member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), who pressed hard in the House of Commons for the Comptroller General.
We must consider whether or not that system is appropriate and whether it can be strengthened. Indeed, I must say to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the President of the Treasury Board that one of the witnesses before the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, the parliamentary reform committee is going to be the Comptroller General of Canada. We will also be calling witnesses from the Treasury Board, which we think is important as we enter into the new part of the work of the Committee with respect to accountability, closing the loop spoken of by Mr. Lambert in his report and, so eloquently, by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) and the Minister's colleague, the Hon. Member for Rosemont (Mr. Lachance), who have filed a very interesting report which 1 commend to the Minister.
We ought not to lose sight of two other legislative aspects in reforming the system-because that is what we are talking about, reforming the system. One is the process of sunset legislation whereby, with respect to each agency of Government, there is a provision that every five or perhaps seven years is a review by Parliament to see whether or not the circumstances causing the creation of an agency still exist or whether they have changed, if an agency's circumstances should change, there is a determination whether its programs are relevant or whether the Canadian public is getting the best for its tax dollar with respect to the services of Government. I must remind the Minister that an important part of the changes in machinery, for which 1 understand he is responsible, involves the entire question of the accountability and control by Parliament of Crown corporations, which are proliferating. One could make a very partisan speech about the proliferation which has occurred over the years. 1 do not intend to do that this Friday afternoon, but it is a fact, concerning which there has been a promise of action by the Government. The Government of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) did bring forward a piece of legislation which was all-encompassing. There is presently a piece of legislation brought forward by the Government which does not go nearly as far and is not nearly as comprehensive; but that is something which has been done to bring this administration under control.
The Minister devoted a great part of his speech to the question of regulatory reform which has been given lip service in Parliament and devotion by certain Members of Parliament. Unfortunately, it has not been a priority of the Government, which is far behind concerning the necessary regulatory reform in the country. It is necessary if we are to make Government relevant, if we are to manage with less in a time of restraint, if
we are to make the process understandable to the business sector and have the business sector appropriately relate to Government. There is a wide gulf of misunderstanding between the private sector and the public sector. I believe reforms in that area can bridge that gulf, because if this country is to prosper, all its elements must come together. The federal Government, the Provinces, the private and public sectors, the private sector including managers, owners, small business and labour, must all come together and the regulatory reform process is of vital concern. It has been addressed by the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, which is co-chaired by a Liberal Senator and a Progressive Conservative Member of Parliament.
I have in my hand the Order Paper, and I am not sure of the number, but 1 believe there are at least six or eight reports, maybe more, involving regulatory reform which have not been addressed by this Parliament or the Government. I want to tell the Minister that the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure is concerned about it, and the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments has indicated to the Special Committee that it wants to come forward to discuss the matter, to link the regulatory reform process with parliamentary reform, because that is indeed what it involves. This institution must have the tools to make the accountability process work. I commend the report to the Minister's attention.
There is another important aspect. I am now referring to the very successful Special Committee on Regulatory Reform which was chaired by the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) and co-chaired by the distinguished Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) and the Hon. Member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook). The Committee produced a benchmark report. Because we are not opposing the Bill, we must be assured today or on other occasions that the report on regulatory reform does not gather dust, but rather gathers interest, and that the labour of the members of that Special Committee, the Hon. Member for the Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish), the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby), the Hon. Member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger) and the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), was not in vain. It is one thing for Members of Parliament to work on these matters, but what is more important is that there be a discernible response from the Government to such reports, which is what the process of parliamentary reform is all about. That is why there is a provision in the third report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, the parliamentary reform committee, that the Government respond in a comprehensive way, not in a piecemeal way. The Committee can request that. I think it is extremely important that that be done. I do not want to see this work lie fallow, because a lot of hard work by these Members whose names 1 have mentioned and other Members of the House of Commons and the Senate will go by the board if it is allowed to slip.
November 19, 1982

What about some of their recommendations? 1 am not going to read them all. I suspected that the Minister might make the speech that he did and 1 have the recommendations in broad terms. There are some 29 of them which I commend to the Minister. There has not been a statement in the House with respect to these regulations since that report has been filed.
I am going to highlight some of them. They say this is part of a reform process. They recommend that Departments and agencies pre-publish regulations whenever that is appropriate. Why? Because those regulations affect the public; they affect business; they affect labour; they affect fishermen; they affect primary producers of all kinds; they affect small and large businesses. They have an impact. How many times has that Committee on Statutory Instruments heard from what 1 call the aggrieved public as a result of the imposition of regulations? These were not passed in bad faith, I have to say, but with bad judgment, I must say, on some occasions.
It would be better if there was a notification and comment process where, if regulations were to be dealt with, they would be prepared, filed and available at the time of second reading, if that were possible. Before a Bill in this House receives third reading, those regulations would be open to the public which is concerned.
There is a suggestion by the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments that perhaps when a statute is sent to Committee to study the merits of a proposal, the regulatory power contained in that statute should be referred to the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments. At that time the extent of the regulatory power, the question as to whether the Government really needs that power to carry out the intention of the statute, could be dealt with.
I am alarmed about the developing process of producing skeletal legislation and leaving so much of it to regulation. That explains partly why in the United Kingdom there were 800 regulations in one particular period of time, and in Canada there were 3,500 regulations in the same period of time. That is a change of policy I commend to the hon. gentleman.
The Committee also said that there should be an impact assessment of these regulations. How will those regulations impact on the sectors that they are meant to govern, because they are legislative in nature?
There was the recommendation by the Committee that each Department and agency review immediately its regulatory statutes and regulations to identify unnecessary and outdated regulatory statutes and regulations. They should set a schedule so that we and the public will know that the process is going on, a process that would lead to more detailed review and further action.
There was also the recommendation that Departments and agencies ensure that all their regulatory activities are evaluated periodically under the program evaluation system administered by the office of the Comptroller General. The Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure has recommended that the annual reports of Departments and agencies
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
be referred automatically to that Committee. I think that is again a benchmark recognition that will do so much for private Members of the House of Commons and for the process of Parliament to hold Government accountable. The Committee dealt with that. They say that in those annual reports of Departments and agencies that would come to Committees automatically, there should be a summary of the progress each year that has been made in regulatory reform, including the reduction of paper burden, initiation of better service to the public and expansion of the notice and consultation procedures. There should be a summary for the Committees of this House of Commons each year of major regulatory initiatives undertaken in the past year; an identification of major regulatory initiatives contemplated and of program evaluations contemplated in the past year; and a schedule of future program evaluations.
A number of sound recommendations from the Special Committee on Regulatory Reform impact quite heavily on the work of the Committee of Standing Orders and Procedures. I am not surprised because there is a general feeling in the community that Parliament and our processes here by which we hold Government accountable are in a state of disrepair, and that the time has come for some significant changes.
There is an interesting recommendation which I want to bring specifically to the attention of the Minister, if I may do so. That was recommendation No. 12. It says that there should be certain procedural requirements for appeals to the Cabinet from the decisions of regulatory agencies. I recommend that the Minister consider that very carefully with his colleagues. The ones that come to mind are the appeals that come from the CRTC with respect to Bell Canada rates. There is a great deal of concern and worry about Bell Canada rates both from the point of view of the consumer and Bell Canada. 1 have always been concerned that there is not full disclosure to the sides involved of the cases of each other.
I recommend that this Government study the processes that are in place in the Government of Ontario. When I was practising at the Bar and I was appealing decisions of regulatory agencies, such as the Ontario Municipal Board or the Ontario Highway Transport Board, I as an appellant had to disclose my case on appeal to the other side. The issues were there, clearly defined, and there was at least some certainty that all of the issues would be before the Cabinet. The Cabinet would be judged, and they are ultimately accountable-on the basis of how they dealt with those issues. Under the present system nobody knows what the cases are. We can guess, but nobody really does know.
It is interesting, too, that preceding the reference which appointed 20 Members of this House of Commons to the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, which I call parliamentary reform, the Committee on Regulatory Reform had acted as an advance guard with respect to the necessity of changing the system in the House. They talked in their report about parliamentary reforms, that the House of Commons be authorized to perform certain functions on their

Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
own initiative without reference from the House of Commons, by the way, which is the gist of the Committee processes in the report that is now standing on the Order Paper, having been tabled by my hon. friend from Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre), who is the chairman of the Parliamentary Reform Committee. It calls for monitoring of the process; a review of the subject matter of new, subordinate legislation; a review of specifically regulatory activities of each federal Department on its own. It goes on and on. It is an important Bill. It is housekeeping, but a very important part of housekeeping, a very important change in the process.
As the Minister is beginning his sojourn in office, I pray that he will not let grass grow under his feet with respect to regulatory reform. I pray he will not do that because subordinate legislation. Orders in Council, regulations, is a growth industry in Canada. It will be commitment by the Government that will take the lead, supported by an equally strong commitment from all political parties in this House of Commons, that can improve the process of considering that aspect of the accountability of Government.
I dare say that if the Minister or his successor is successful, whether that successor for the purpose of this debate comes from this side or that side of the House-and 1 think it will be from this side-it will tend to do a great deal to bridge the gap of misunderstanding that now exists between the public sector, the Public Service and the broad Canadian public. I think that effort is worthwhile and that is the spirit with which we approach this Bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be extremely brief. We welcome the move by the Government to eliminate from the statute books legislation which is no longer applicable. The majority of Canadians find it difficult enough to deal with the laws that still apply without having to make their way through laws which are not applicable.
I want to suggest to the Minister a simple process that would make it much easier for all of us to do our work. In the future when we are faced with Bills such as this to repeal certain statutes-and I certainly hope we will be-I suggest as a matter of reform that the Bill read exactly the same in French as in English. That is one of the difficulties with this Bill; I am sure the Minister is aware of it. Although the French Bill and the English Bill are the same, they appear in a different order.
Anyone trying to make sure that what was repealed in English was indeed repealed in French must do far more work than is absolutely necessary. The example I would give is quite clear. The section dealing with the Ministry of Veterans Affairs appears as the second paragraph of the French text and is No. 3. The same section in English appears in the final part of the English text and is No. 124.
We should try to simplify things. That means eliminating obsolete statutes and wiping from the books obsolete regulations. It also means making it possible for people concerned and interested to be able to do so as easily and readily as
possible. I do not pretend for a moment that it is a major concern. Neither do I expect the Minister to respond other than to note it for ease of handling.
In the process of determining the obsolete legislation in the future, in order to ease the process and to answer those who are concerned about such matters, in addition to the Bill there could be an explanation given at the time the Bill is tabled for first reading, listing the various statutes and the reason why, whether they have been superseded, outlived their usefulness or have in one way or another become redundant.
If that explanation could be provided by the Ministries involved, there would be no question in anyone's mind as to the appropriateness of the action being taken either by the Minister in charge or the House of Commons. I would hate to agree to repeal and Act only to discover down the road some obscure reason why we ought not to have done so. I do not suggest that every piece of legislation that appears here need take a great deal of time and discussion as to whether it is still useful. It would ease the process for lawyers when Bills are repealed to know the substantive reason. That kind of information should be readily available at the time of first reading of a Bill. It would be available to them and other jurisdictions for their quick perusal and comment.
I hope this is the first in a long series of similar kinds of legislation. I hope we cull out legislation that no longer need be on the books. I am confident that we carry laws that years ago ought to have been done away with.
It may well be that we require, as the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) quite correctly said, to devote some time looking at the recommendations contained in the Committee's report to see whether there is some ongoing work that could be done which would enable the House of Commons to reduce the number of laws presently in force in this country that no longer have evident applicability.
Beyond that, I would be delighted to pass this bill and get on to dealing with other matters that have much more significance and importance.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to rise in the House today to speak on what is really the first step in our Government's long-term commitment to the process of regulatory reform. The step we are taking today is significant not because it is repealing a number of obsolete statutes which are on the books, but because it is the first step in what many of us feel has been too slow a process in bringing about the necessary regulatory reforms in order that we can efficiently operate as a Government, as a House and as a Parliament. Even more important, we can reduce the burden of regulation on the private sector.
I am particularly grateful to the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) for his very generous comments about the work of the Committee on Regulatory Reform. He is a Member of this House who for many years, in a very non-
November 19, 1982

partisan way, has sought to change the procedures by which we work so that we can all do a more effective job for the electorate.
If I could just go back to some of the fundamentals, many Members from all sides of the House have requested, in terms of our reporting on regulatory reform, that two basic objectives be pursued. One is to increase the opportunity for the private sector to participate in the decision-making process before regulations are brought forward by the Government. This requires notice of what the Government's regulatory intentions might be. The second is to give the private sector the opportunity to comment, consult, be heard and come up with alternative suggestions to achieve the most cost-effective way of accomplishing the necessary public goals that are necessary.
In terms of this major part of our recommendations, and we have many specifics dealing with it, I believe we have made some progress, but not sufficient. A number of Departments and agencies have already implemented this process of notice and consultation on a very effective basis. Based on our recommendations and based, I believe, just on good amendment practices, others have started to implement these types of notice and consultation procedures.
I would like to make special reference here to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), and particularly to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), who has published a book on new consultative procedures in dealing with the Department of the Environment. He has also introduced funding for people who want to come to Ottawa to make their views known on particular regulatory measures. I would like to see every Department and agency adopt that type of outward-looking process, and 1 commend the Minister of the Environment on taking the initiative.
I also commend the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for the efforts he has made regarding the increase in funding which is going to public interest groups. Too often, as Hon. Members are aware, it is only the very well heeled, the very rich, who have the staff and the funds available to keep track of what is happening in provincial capitals and our National Capital. They can afford to send the experts, either hired or on staff, to Ottawa to make their views known and to work with our officials in a co-operative effort.
The regulatory process and the making of regulations is adversarial, at least in nature. Sometimes there are winners and sometimes there are losers. On one side it could be business. On the other side it could be consumers. We are concerned about worker health and safety, which costs money. We are concerned about rate increases which are going to have impact upon people who use our telephones, our railways, or whatever.
People who are not well organized and might not have the funds to come forward and make their views known must have that opportunity. We must aid the various methods which we have outlined to provide the public interest groups throughout our society, concerned citizens, people who do have the interest and knowledge, who do have a very important impact to make,
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
the means of participating in this very important process of consultation. We look forward in the days ahead to seeing these notice and consultation procedures expanded to every Department and agency which have not already adopted them.
The second major thrust of our report was that you cannot have effective regulation-making process, one which involves notice and consultation, unless you also have a certain degree of accountability. We looked at the question of accountability and felt that this House, under its present procedures, would be helpless, that it would be hopeless to attempt to take on added responsibilities. We heard testimony to the effect that some Departments have been waiting for four years to make even simple changes to our legislation. Because we are bogged down and have not yet come to grips with how we can expedite the work of this House, we felt the proper way to proceed would be to look at the Committee system of Parliament to see if the expertise on those Committees could be utilized in a constructive way to help in the regulation-making process. We therefore suggested that for a brief period of time a Special Committee would oversee the implementation of regulatory reform in Canada at the federal level. Then, on an ongoing basis, the existing Standing Committees would have the responsibility of ensuring that Departments and agencies were introducing the regulatory reforms, and in certain cases they would even have the opportunity to look into the substance of regulations which have come forward.
I am sorry to say that to date we have not yet seen that type of role evolve in our Committees. But I am heartened, Mr. Speaker, by the fact that the report of the Committee looking into parliamentary reform, which was published some two weeks ago, goes a long way in dealing with this particular issue. We have waited a long time, but it is a good report because it gives added power to the Committees. It has adopted many of the recommendations which were set forth in Chapter 6 and every one of the most important ones. The Committees will be smaller, will have limited substitution, and will have the ability to develop the expertise to look at all aspects of the regulations. These Committees will have people on them who are committed to dealing with the matter. They will have the tools as well as the research people, and they will have the ability to travel.
The question we still have to examine is whether the automatic reference of an annual report of Departments and agencies is going to be adequate to allow the subject matter with which we are concerned to be discussed on what I believe will be a very non-partisan and highly constructive basis. I think the example with respect to the working of these Committees in the future is set by the task forces. They were small, and although they included Members from all sides of this House, there was very seldom disagreement. They worked in a very non-partisan way. I speak for many people who are backbenchers on this side of the House when 1 say they feel their great talents and expertise can be far better utilized in the Committee system if they have these reforms. Their input would be constructive and meaningful.

We look forward very much to the implementation of this plan. I hope for the support of all sides of this Elouse for a new process by which the Committee system becomes a very integral part. In fact the front arm of the legislative branch, dealing with representations of private sector groups, not only from business but from labour, consumers' interests groups, people concerned with the environment and with worker health and safety.
I applaud the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) who has brought forward this measure today. He has under his jurisdiction the responsibility of the office of the co-ordinator of regulatory reform, continuing along the steps which have been commenced. It is very frustrating, Mr. Speaker, perhaps because I am a relatively new Member of this House of Commons, to see the slowness with which the tortoise of change moves along the road. I would be better reconciled to its slowness, Mr. Speaker, if in the future I could be assured that its course will be steadfast-that the path taken by the President of the Treasury Board, which is supported enthusiastically by my Minister, the Hon. Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston), will be supported and encouraged by all Members on both sides of this House.

I, indeed, enthusiastically support any Bill that repeals existing laws. In fact, if he would like to add a whole bunch more, I would enthusiastically support that. If you look at the two extremes of repealing none and repealing all the laws, you would err less if you repealed them all.
On the question of regulatory reform, which certainly is supported, I have a question. Just how seriously is the Government committed to this process? Four or five years ago, Mr. Speaker, I saw an estimate of the cost of regulation in Canada. It was estimated at that time that the cost of regulation to the Canadian economy was something like $15 billion per year, and it was a terrible burden then on the Canadian economy. Since that time it has certainly not gone down. If no new regulations or interventions have been added, it would amount to about $25 billion in today's dollars, which is terribly costly.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before one o'clock I indicated that both 1 and my party did not disagree-in fact we enthusiastically agree-with the idea that obsolete, unused, archaic and useless statutes on the law books of Canada should be repealed. Nobody can disagree with that. But in listening to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) describing this Government's motivation for introducing this Bill, I had to question his contention that somehow introduction of this Bill represents a significant or sincere move in the area of deregulation which is supposedly a policy of this Government.
As I indicated, Mr. Speaker, some years ago an independent consulting group, 1 think it was called the resource group, did a study of regulation in Canada and concluded that Government regulation cost the Canadian economy $15 billion a year. Now, just taking into account inflation and neglecting the fact that we have had scads of regulation since then, the cost today would be $25 billion spent on regulation. Almost every economist, Mr. Speaker, who has looked at the Canadian economy-indeed, the Government itself-has concluded that one of the severe problems this country faces is lack of productivity. We are simply not as productive as the Japanese or the Americans. Indeed, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development we are twenty-third on a list of 23 countries when it comes to productivity.
Now, what does that mean? Does it mean that Canadian workers do not work as hard as workers in other countries? Certainly not. What it means is that we do a heck of a lot of things in this country which produce nothing. One of those things is dealing with Government regulations. Three years ago I was in Japan, Mr. Speaker. It was a real eye opener for me. It is an amazing country; a pile of rock, they cannot feed themselves, they have virtually no arable land, no natural resources, but they have tremendous growth and prosperity. Their productivity performance is incredible.
I asked the Canadian Ambassador, who had been there for a number of years, what the Japanese have that we do not have. How are they able to do this? Well, he said, for one thing they have only 10,000 lawyers in the whole country. He said that only half in jest. The fact is that in this country the two growth industries or professions are law and accounting, because we do nothing in this place but make work for those professions.
In a similar vein, I was reading a story in The Atlantic Review about the deindustrialization of the American economy. The author of the article asked someone what had happened, when did the United States start losing competition to the Japanese. The man drew two lines on a graph, one going from the lower left to the upper right representing the number of graduate lawyers each year; the other one went from the upper left to the lower right representing the number of electrical engineers graduating each year. The two lines crossed in 1970, which is precisely the time at which the Japanese started outperforming the Americans very significantly. That, Mr. Speaker, is the problem in the United States.
November 19, 1982

The problem here is twice that. It amazes me how we sit around and think about productivity and what we are going to do about it. We gnash our teeth and wring our hands over our inability to compete, and our answer is to hire a lawyer to head a Royal Commission and make more work for lawyers. Our answer to every problem is to create more paper work and burden the country with more regulation.
The difficulty I have, in its most fundamental sense, and the most severe criticism that I can make of the Government opposite, is the frequency with which its actions are contrary to its policy statements. In this area of regulatory reform there is no better example. The Minister said proudly that in the Treasury Board there was the regulatory reform commission which had been working for a number of years. What did it produce? It produced this list of laws which should be abolished or repealed, laws such as the White Phosphorous Matches Act. I know there are dozens of lawyers out there looking at this Act daily to be guided in their actions! Then there is The Business Profits War Tax Act, 1916. Thank goodness we do not have to worry about that any more! Thank goodness that burden of regulation is being lifted from the Canadian economy, because it will give such a spurt! When we look down the list we see they are all like that. Sure, they should be abolished, but to claim that it is deregulation is to stretch the truth beyond reason.
In the last four or five years the stated policy of the Liberal Party has been deregulation. We had the introduction of the National Energy Program which, among other things, created three new Government agencies-one dealing with COR, one dealing with PIP, and one dealing with offshore Canadian oil and gas land administration.
Incidentally, I could have mentioned the Canadian Benefits Committee, that joint interdepartmental Committee, and others, but I should like to deal with these three. So far the agency dealing with PIP has 100 employees and the COR Agency has 400 employees. The regulations put out by these three organizations measure in inches, not in centimeters. There is a pile of regulations which has been put out by these three newly-created agencies. The cost to the private sector created by these brand-new agencies of Government is in the tens of millions, in the form of new lawyers, accountants and paper shufflers of various sorts hired to deal with them.
Historically in oil companies-and I am talking about the upstream end of the business where they are drilling for oil and gas-for every three geologists they needed one paper shuffler. The geologists are the people who go out and look for oil and tell the companies where to drill. As a result of the Government's actions, that ratio is reversed. For every geologist, companies now need three paper shufflers to handle the regulations, application forms, etc. This is a totally nonproductive, bureaucratic, regulatory burden.
This is also one of the reasons Canada is twenty-third on a list of 23 countries when it comes to productivity. It is offensive to decency and common sense to listen to the President of the Treasury Board say that the Government is committed to deregulation, that it is working on it, and that this is an
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
example of the fine work which is being done. Yet on the other side of the coin we have the creation of bureaucratic red tape and monstrous regulatory burden by another Department of Government, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. The fact is that the left hand does not know what the other left hand is doing. It is hypocrisy at best. One wonders what it will require to force the executive and the bureaucrats to follow the policy statements of the Government. Why is there such a divergence between promise and performance? Why are there always statements of policies here and actions there?
The closest literary reference to that kind of behaviour which I could find was in George Orwell's "1984", the doublespeak or the mispeak activities of government as a way of controlling the masses, to ensure that everyone pays due respect to and has fear of the government. This is exactly what we have here. They are for deregulation, but on the other hand they create three new agencies with six inches of regulation for people who want to be in business in Canada. If this continues, instead of being in twenty-third place we will be the fortieth out of 40 countries; we will continue to deteriorate and be unable to compete with Japan, the United States and European countries. Also we will continue to see a drop in the standard of living and high unemployment. In other words, we will continue in the economic mess and doldrums in which we have been for far too long.
Instead of appointing Royal Commissions, new advisory committees or hiring new advisers, the Government should fire the 3,500-odd policy analysts in the Public Service who spend their time looking for problems and solutions to them. The Government should do what is promised, namely, cut back on excessive regulatory burdens. If the Government did what it promised, it would give the economy a boost and give the 1.5 million unemployed people some real hope for the first time in many years.
We have no objections to the Bill except to the extent that it is probably not long enough in terms of the list of laws which should be repealed. There are many other laws which should be added to the list. Perhaps we will have some worth-while suggestions for the Minister in Committee. If the bureaucrats will allow him to listen to suggestions from mere elected people, perhaps there will be some further improvement.

Mr. Speaker, first 1 should like to echo the sentiments expressed by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), but also I should like to indicate that I am entering this debate in a rather disappointed fashion. While the redundant legislation which is being repealed is certainly a step in the right direction, the Minister described at length the progress made in the area of regulatory reform. Certainly the track record of the Government is disappointing, to say the least and to be charitable.
In these times of economic difficulty we should get serious about regulatory reform. It is quite clear that regulatory

November 19, 1982
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
reform has not been a priority of the Government. It is time for action, rather than further talk and examination. It probably goes beyond the stage of simply requesting regulatory reform. We are looking for regulatory house cleaning. This will clearly require joint action by the two levels of Government, and perhaps even the municipalities which are involved as well.
In these times it is necessary to exercise restraint, to reduce business and Government overhead, to enhance producitvity, to be more innovative, more creative and more competitive. These are all crucial elements on the road to recovery. I firmly believe that excessive regulation which exists in the country at all levels has stymied the creative and innovative spirit of Canadians. It has caused our products to be too expensive in terms of penetrating international markets. It has resulted in Canada having a system of Government and control that is far too expensive commensurate with our level of economic growth and wealth in this country.
It seems to me that if we are going to improve our over-all economic performance, we have to grapple with this issue on an emergency basis. We all know that in this country industry has been forced to scale down its operation. Roy Phillips, President of the CMA, has said:
-while Canada's manufacturing sector, which employs about 20 per cent of the work force, has lost about 255,000 jobs in the last year, bureaucracies have grown. While Manufacturing jobs fell to under 2 million-with similar losses in associated sectors which supply manufacturing-the three levels of government hired another 25,000 more people-
Those salaries are really part and parcel of the overhead burden in our country.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton made reference to the recommendations of the Special Committee on Regulatory Reform. There are some 29 of them in total. These are very good recommendations and they represent a lot of hard work, commitment and dedication by Members of this House. But really nothing has happened. The document containing the recommendations sits there and basically gathers dust.
The Economic Council of Canada, that permanent Royal Commission, did an extensive examination of the regulatory process in this country. It produced a document entitled "Reforming Regulation in 1981". That report advanced some 66 specific recommendations. I happen to be interested in it because it deals at length with the regulatory burden in transportation. Twenty-five of those recommendations had to do with the transportation sector. In a general way, this Economic Council of Canada report concluded that Canadians are overregulated. This overregulation results in inefficiency, waste and higher prices. The report further recommended that the economy be stripped of wasteful, damaging regulations and that incentives, rather than punishment, be used to respond to social concerns. Unfortunately, I know of no recommendation advanced in this particular document that has been put into effect. The report merely gathers dust.
When we have an announcement, as we did this past week, of a Royal Commission on the economy, I really wonder what it does to undercut and undermine the status of the Economic Council of Canada, which is an ongoing Royal Commission charged with the responsibility of providing economic advice to the Government and, indeed, to Parliament.
Here we have an institution that is funded by the taxpayers of Canada. It is independent. It does excellent work, but nobody pays any attention to it. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre, talked about the costs of the regulatory burden in Canada. He mentioned a figure in the order of $20 billion to $25 billion. We know that it runs to the billions of dollars, but it is rather difficult to identify with any degree of accuracy. But on the basis of learned assumptions it would seem that figure of $20 billion to $25 billion is not inaccurate.
I had an opportunity to do some research in this particular field. Some companies and industries have, in fact, assessed the regulatory burden in their own operation. Bell Canada assessed its costs of the regulatory burden imposed upon it to range in the order of $35 million to $50 million annually, all of which I might add is passed on to the consumer. Dow Chemical in 1978 monitored its regulatory burden and arrived at a figure of some $20 million. Again, I remind Hon. Members that this $20 million is a cost of doing business and is imposed upon the consumer.
This report dealt rather extensively with the trucking industry. The Economic Council of Canada stated that the licensing process in the trucking industry alone-just the licensing process-costs the industry some $40 million annually. That amount is in addition to huge indirect costs associated with the regulations regarding back haul, load limits, the right to haul to certain destinations and the right not to haul to certain destinations. These restrictions create grave inefficiencies in the system and result in the freight rate being exorbitantly high.
I am told on good authority that when the United States deregulated its trucking industry the fleet capacity increased by 50 per cent without adding one new vehicle to the fleet. It was found under the regime of regulations in place that essentially the trucks were running with a 50 per cent load factor at all times. With the scaling down or removal of regulation, the trucks were able to haul from point A to point B and from point B to point A. As a result, with the back hauls and the rationalization that occurred, it has had the effect of bringing down freight rates in the United States.
Yes, there has been some rationalization in the trucking industry. Some trucking companies went out of business. But if we are really serious about maximizing our efficiency and getting the best bang for the buck, we will have to take a look at that. Some industries have become excessively fat as a result of hiding behind the burden of regulation. That ripples right across the North American continent.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre, talked about the impact of the National Energy Program. It has been
November 19, 1982

suggested that the result of the imposition of these new regulatory agencies and the administration of the National Energy Program will result in some $1.5 billion spent in supervising and regulating the oil industry over the next eight years. Here again there is a direct cost which has to be paid for by someone. That someone is usually the consumer or the taxpayer, in both cases the same person, the one faced with paying the shot.
Let us take a look at direct administrative costs. Taking five rather high profile industries in existence at the present time, the CTC, the National Energy Board, the CRTC, the Atomic Energy Control Board and FIR A, their administrative costs run to approximately $100 million a year. The CTC alone costs about $30 million in administrative costs. These costs are increasing. They have increased anywhere from 25 per cent to 40 per cent over the last three years.
These regulatory industries are supposed to protect the consumer as far as prices are concerned. We now know that really quite the opposite has happened. The recent Statistics Canada report which was leaked-I am not sure if it has been officially published-indicated that those prices which are regulated by agencies on a year-to-year basis have increased, from April to April, at a rate of 17 per cent to 18 per cent over the last year. At the same time, however, prices which are not regulated have increased by roughly 9 per cent. What is the reason for that? The unregulated prices are subject to the vagaries of the marketplace in which they must compete.
It is interesting to note that the consumer price index component of regulated prices amounts to aproximately 25 per cent. Therefore, 25 per cent of the CPI is composed of prices that are regulated by some agency, either federal or provincial. We can only conclude that these agencies are in fact largely contributing to the inflationary pressures that we are trying to deal with and this is certainly not in the best interests of the consumer.
Another matter of concern is the fact that political decisions are being imposed upon the regulatory agencies with increasing frequency. This has the result of usurping, ignoring or upstaging the role of the decision-making bodies and, in many cases, many of these regulatory agencies have become agencies of convenience used as a vehicle to delay a decision, find out information or leave the impression that the public is being heard. The entire exercise is becoming somewhat of a farce.
I am glad the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) is in the House because a clear example of this is the case of the VIA Rail cut-backs. In that instance, Canadian rail passenger service was cut back by 20 per cent with the simple stroke of a ministerial pen. That action reversed an earlier CTC decision which was made after two years of extensive study and consultation with the public. After much public input, a decision on a route structure was made which seemed to be in the best interests of the travelling public and, indeed, in the best interests of Canada. A year later the Minister simply usurped that decision with the stroke of a pen. So the CTC process was
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
essentially useless. A lot of money, time and effort was spent when, ultimately, the Minister ended up making a decision by decree.

speechtext: We proved that it would not work that way.

speechtext:
I hope the Minister becomes involved in the debate. I would like to hear him challenge that particular observation.
Another example of political decisions being imposed upon regulatory agencies concerns the Bell Canada rate. The ratesetting process of the CRTC was abruptly circumvented when the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) announced back in August that the Bell rate would be limited to a 6 per cent and 5 per cent level. Again, the regulatory process was circumvented.
Another example deals with branch lines. The predecessor to the Minister of Transport, the Hon. Otto Lang, circumvented the CTC process in 1975. On this occasion, 1 think it was done to the advantage of individual farmers, He unilaterally decided that he would insert particular branch lines into the permanent railway network. He proceeded with this decision without the advice of the CTC. Once again, the CTC was circumvented. It played an insignificant role in that decision.
A more recent example concerns the STOL service between Toronto, Montreal and Ottawa. On August 10, 1982 the current Minister of Transport reversed an earlier CTC decision allowing STOL service. After three years of hearings and intensive public discussions, the CTC found that the applicants failed satisfactorily to meet the criterion of public convenience and necessity. The Cabinet decided, however, that there were compelling reasons and benefits that would make the project desirable and thereby approved it. Again, so much for the regulatory process.
There are many examples to demonstrate the fact that the regulatory agencies are really being used in a manner which makes the whole process something of a farce. 1 suggest that we should perhaps consider those agencies in that light. It becomes quite clear that the best laid plans and regulations are being transcended by political decisions with increased frequency.
Another observation that one must make is that the utopian ideal that everything we do can be planned and regulated to perfection has clearly been discredited. As well, we must realize that regulatory agencies go through a natural process of decay. I believe they become too cumbersome and that the administrative overload becomes very costly. In that deteriorating process the agencies themselves, in many cases, become ineffective and unresponsive to the decisions that they are supposed to make. In some cases they end up lacking in independence.
An interesting illustration of that concerns the airlines and the question of deep discount fares. This is a classic example of the agency being captured by the industry it was regulating. The airlines themselves asked the CTC to intervene and disallow the deep discount fares because they were taking a

November 19, 1982
Miscellaneous Statute Repeal Act
heavy toll on their balance sheet. In this case the agency is being captured by the industry that it was intended to regulate.
I suggest it is time for us to stop kidding ourselves. It is time for a major regulatory house cleaning in this country. I believe that many of the regulations and the agencies have outlived their usefulness. Some should be eliminated or at least scaled down or restructured. There is no question that when we are experiencing these very difficult economic times we can clearly identify a number of areas where the regulatory burden, and the burden of government itself, is having very negative effect upon business and commerce in this country without protecting the consumers' needs.
In conclusion, 1 would like to make some suggestions to the Minister. First, he should consider the recommendation made by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association which has called for a two-year moratorium on new regulations which would do nothing to contribute to the economic growth of this country. Second, I believe he should give serious consideration, since the regulatory issue is one which must be tackled at both the federal and provincial levels of Government, to establishing something similar to a federal-provincial deregulation commission. A commission such as that could be charged with the task of untangling the bureaucratic web across the country, reducing duplication and bringing about greater uniformity. Its basic goal would be to remove those barriers which stifle competition, innovation and efficiency and strangle commeri-cal enterprise in this country. This suggestion warrants his careful consideration because much groundwork has already been done. However, it will clearly require the co-operation of both levels of Government, and the provincial Governments are just as guilty of this as the federal Government. If we are to attack some of the structural problems in our economy, it would be a good idea to start demonstrating that the two levels of Government can co-operate in the best interests of commerce and enterprise in this country.
I would like to refer to my third recommendation. When I am speaking about scaling down regulation, I am not advocating total deregulation. However, in the course of this review, this rationalization, we must always ensure that provisions are made to protect consumers and to ensure that the public has meaningful access by which it may make its case. The public must have the opportunity to be heard so that its interest may be protected, particularly as they relate to safety matters. This is particularly true where there is a monopolistic or captive situation. There must be a clear opportunity for the consumer and the public at large to have a say in this process.
The Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton alluded to what would be my fourth recommendation. I believe that all regulations and all regulatory agencies should carry a sunset provision calling for a periodic review. This is really the first piece of legislation brought here during the 14 years I have been in the House which has repealed a significant number of Bills or laws. That is clearly a step in the right direction. We should have the sunset provisions in our regulations with respect to the agencies administering those regulations. We have a habit of churning out legislation, creating new bureaucracies and
