that Bill C-96, to amend the Financial Administration Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to move second reading today of Bill C-96, the purpose of which is to amend the Financial Administration Act in order to enable Treasury Board further to improve financial control and accountability in departments and agencies of the Government of Canada.
The last major revision to the Financial Administration Act was undertaken in the late 1960s. Since that time a number of important recommendations and agreements concerning
Financial Administration Act
financial administration matters have been made requiring further legislative change. These amendments are included in the Bill. They stem from reports by successive Auditors General recommending specific improvements in a number of aspects of financial administration. Also they stem from the 1975 study of the Accounts of Canada which recommended change to certain budgetary, accounting and reporting practices which for a long time have caused concern about their effect on parliamentary control of expenditures, and from a variety of proposals for making amendments to clarify the intent of the legislation where difficulties in its application have been experienced.
There has also been a request from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) to include several items dealing with government banking and borrowing.
In addition to these externally generated initiatives for change, the Office of the Comptroller General has identified other areas where legislative change is needed. While the majority of items in this Bill are administrative and technical improvements, there are a number of amendments which 1 should like to mention today because of the important improvements they will enable us to implement.
The first significant amendment concerns the proposals for the future treatment of uncollectible debts due to the Crown. As Members may know, Section 18 of the Act at present authorizes the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Treasury Board to make regulations authorizing deletions from the accounts of obligations due to Her Majesty not exceeding $5,000. Deletion of debts over $5,000 requires parliamentary approval.
Section 18 was last changed in 1969. An analysis of the submissions for deletion for a recent one-year period revealed 1,528 cases between $2,000 and $5,000, for a total of $4.8 million, and an additional 1,344 cases over $5,000, for a total of $28.8 million. Although statistics suggest that an increase in the limit from $5,000 to $100,000 would eliminate much of the administrative burden associated with parliamentary approval, and it was recommended that the limit should be removed from the Act and put in regulations where it could be subject to periodic revision.
While it is true that the existing law reserves for Parliament the authority to write off debts, it should be understood that this change is intended to deal administratively rather than legislatively with a variety of relatively small amounts which have proved to be uncollectible. Generally speaking, these include taxes receivable, accounts receivable, accountable advances and a variety of minor items for various purposes. As this type of debt is actually unrealized revenue, it is recorded on a memorandum basis only in the records of a Department, and deletion has no effect on the expenditures of government.

November 19, 1982
Financial Administration Act
Where an item was initially authorized by Parliament through estimates, such as a loan or investment, and that item is on the Statement of Assets and Liabilities of Canada, any amount written off, no matter how large or small, will continue to require legislative approval prior to making an adjustment. Large dollar value items are usually in this category.
I should like to remind the House that any debt which is to be written off under the proposed regulations would be required by law to be reported in the Public Accounts.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the changes to Section 18 will reinforce the Government's continuing efforts to collect vigorously all revenues and debts due the Crown.
Another amendment concerns loan guarantees. The requirement to provide loan guarantees has arisen on occasion, and the authority to provide these guarantees was obtained through the estimates process because it was considered to be a financial matter and it would not have been realistic to amend program legislation.
If program legislation had a clause authorizing loan guarantees, there would be no need to bring specific items before Parliament. The process now used provides Members of Parliament with an opportunity to review each specific item in committee and to register their concerns, their points of view, and their support if they wish to do so.
Because it is desirable to continue to have Parliament approve requests for loan guarantees, an amendment to Section 22 will allow for the continued use of estimates, that is, appropriation acts, to obtain such authority.
There is an amendment to Section 25 concerning the existing statutory requirement for the certification and recording of financial commitments, which was legislated some time ago. This requirement was met with the Comptroller of the Treasury as the central point for the control of disbursements of public money. As a result of the recommendations of the Glassco Commission in 1962, the position of the Comptroller of the Treasury was abolished and responsibility for, among other things, commitment certification and accounting was given to Departments.
Over the past several years commitment accounting practices in Departments have been addressed in several government-wide studies. There was the Report of the Auditor General of Canada on Financial Management of Canada. There was the Report on the Study of the Accounts of Canada, a study carried out interdepartmentally on the various purposes served by those accounts.
In 1980 the Government announced the creation of the Policy and Expenditure Management System. This system recognizes that policy and program decisions must be taken in the context of, and with the responsibility for, costs and expenditure limitations. The creation of resource envelopes and long-term plans that will provide Departments with a context within which they can examine future costs of ongoing programs and new initiatives is central to the new system. It follows, therefore, that multi-year financial arrangements must not only be considered in terms of the budget year
operational plan but also within the limits set out in the multiyear operational plans.
These facts, plus the introduction of the Policy and Expenditure Management System, suggested the need for a specific and detailed review of Section 25. Therefore, the office of the Comptroller General of Canada launched an extensive review of commitment certification and accounting practices. This review revealed that there are three major problems which create inefficiencies and weaken control over financial obligations entered into on behalf of the Government of Canada. It was found that present Section 25 is not relevant to statutory appropriations. It was found also that the section does not require control over multi-year arrangements and it requires unnecessary costly procedures to control small-value commitments.
In summary, these three problems can be traced to the present legislation, which is the underlying cause of most of the shortcomings identified in previous government-wide studies. Therefore, it has been concluded that the method of controlling commitments should not be in the legislative wording of the Act. The proposed amendment will, however, continue the requirement for control over commitments, but the methods by which that control will be kept will be the subject of Treasury Board policy direction rather than law. I believe the new policy direction will strengthen control over financial commitments while at the same time effecting economies in administrative overhead. It will do so by emphasizing, for statutory appropriations, the need for determination of eligibility prior to payment rather than commitment certification as to fund availability. It will also relate commitment control to the reference levels approved for departmental multi-year operational plans for future fiscal years as well as the current fiscal year.
Section 30 of the Act is being amended to provide better disclosure and improved accountability on the use of budgetary and non-budgetary appropriations on which Parliament has imposed annual ceilings. In general, the amendment would require debts incurred prior to the end of the fiscal year for work performed, goods received, services rendered or debts resulting from contractual arrangements to be recorded as charges to appropriations, even if the inclusion of such charges would result in total charges exceeding the appropriation.
The Section is being amended in conformity with a recommendation of the Study of the Accounts of Canada, which recommendation, as you may recall, was endorsed by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. This amendment, in addition, addresses the concerns of successive Auditors General respecting the non-reporting of the over-utilization of appropriations.
Although Section 30 is proposed to be amended to permit the recording of charges in excess of appropriations, 1 want to stress that the amendment is essentially a recording and reporting mechanism; the requirement of the Government to respect the annual ceiling of appropriation authority granted by Parliament is by no means relaxed. Accordingly, charges in
November 19, 1982

excess of an appropriation will only be discharged if parliamentary authority to do so exists.
I want to mention, by way of conclusion, that since Bill C-96 was tabled for first reading last March, the Government has received a number of comments and suggestions. We have studied all of these very carefully, and in several cases we are agreeing to the suggestions and therefore intend to make appropriate recommendations for changes at the committee stage. These changes include the deletion of Section 20.1 dealing with net voting; Section 101 dealing with interdepartmental charging; and Section 102 dealing with the charging and paying of interest. As well, there will be a number of technical amendments to wording. For the most part we are accepting these changes on the basis of legal advice that they do not in any way undermine our important policy objectives for improved financial control which can be attained within existing legislation.
These are the main issues contained in this Bill, and because of the great interest shown by Members of the House in tightening the whole area of financial accountability and in response to recommendations of the Auditors General over the years and of the Public Accounts Committee, I ask Members of the House to support this Bill for second reading and reference to the committee.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-96 is a Bill which comes before the House from time to time and seems rather technical in nature but one which is routine and which perhaps should slip through the parliamentary process without undue examination or consideration.
However, a closer examination of the details of this Bill shows that it is, in fact, much more than routine. The manner in which Parliament examines and controls Government spending through the estimates and through the appropriation Act, Acts that come in at the end of a supply period, changed very profoundly in 1969 with the introduction of new rules to the House, by closure I might add. A provision was introduced to our Standing Orders which dictated that when estimates are brought in-after the money has already been spent in many cases-there is a certain period of time in which the estimates could be examined. At the end of that time they are deemed to be reported to the House, and on that last day a bill is introduced to appropriate the funds for those expenditures. That Bill is passed without debate or consideration. There is no provision for debate or amendment to any part of the Appropriation Act. In fact, it is an automatic rubber stamp and it is a farce to call the Appropriation Act an Act of Parliament in the same sense as other Acts of Parliament are passed.
Prior to that time it was the habit of Governments to use the Appropriation Act's mechanism as a method of making minor adjustments and changes in law via what we call dollar items. When there was an opportunity to discuss and amend the Appropriation Act, perhaps this was not an undesirable or extreme situation as long as it was not done to excess, because
Financial Administration Act
it would then involve omnibus legislation. But if debate served as an administrative aid, it was proper.
Once rule changes were brought in by closure which denied the opportunity for debate and amendment to the Appropriation Act, it became most inappropriate for the Government and its bureaucrats to use that vehicle to introduce new legislation and ideas. When that change was introduced, the bureaucrats continued to use that vehicle to bring in those laws it wished. Various Members of the House objected to that procedure. They did so formally on March 10, 1971, on December 10, 1973, on March 6, 1974, on June 22, 1976, on March 22, 1977, on June 7, 1977, and several times since then. They raised objections to the Speaker by indicating that this type of procedure was improper and in violation of what parliamentary authority is all about.
Various Speakers, including Mr. Speaker Lamoureux, Mr. Speaker Jerome and, most recently, Madam Speaker Sauve, acknowledged that this was not proper. Mr. Speaker Lamoureux expressed concern about that procedure on several occasions. That did not stop the Treasury Board or the bureaucrats from continuing to use it. They just proceeded, ignoring the clear expression of concern from the House.
Mr. Speaker Jerome underlined and emphasized those concerns and said, "Please do not abuse the House and continue to use that technique to circumvent Parliament and the legislative process." That did not faze the Treasury Board or the bureaucrats at all. They continued to do so.
Finally last June, after compiling this support which had gone back over a decade, argument was presented to Madam Speaker Sauve. She agreed that it had gone on for too long. All of her warnings and those of her predecessors had been ignored for too long. It was time to act and declare that mechanism out of order and unacceptable. She struck down many of the votes in the estimates and potential items in the Appropriation Act that had been put forward by the Treasury Board and the bureaucrats who were trying to abuse the House as they constantly do.
On Wednesday afternoon the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Collenette) praised me in the House for the effort at that time and the decision of the Chair with respect to what happened. He said that it was the only proper decision to make. But does that faze those people, the bureaucrats, who really run the country? Does it faze the young Liberals, those manipulators, those people hired by Michael Pitfield to tell us what to do? It does not faze them one bit. They simply wrote another bill, Bill C-96, which proposes to force a law through Parliament to let them do what Parliament has been saying for the last ten years was improper.
That is exactly the purpose of this Bill. What must we do to restore parliamentary democracy to this country? How frequently will those nameless, faceless manipulators continue doing this? When will the House say no? We are the elected representatives. Perhaps that does not make us as important as those who are appointed, but it should, if you believe in democracy.

I am shocked and ashamed of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) who has allowed himself to be manipulated in this way. I suggest to the President of the Treasury Board that this is his opportunity to stand up and demonstrate that he is his own man, that he does have a backbone and has respect for the House and our institutions. It is hard for me to comprehend the poll results we have been hearing. The latest shows that the Conservatives are leading, with about 46 per cent to the Liberals' 30 per cent and the NDPs' 21 per cent. Returning to the matter of security and stability that we once knew, at one time children, the elderly and even people going to and from work, felt safe. However, now people who return home late from work cause alarm to those at home because it is feared that something may have happened to them. Such fear was unheard of not too long ago. Today, we are advocating not only that we lock our doors, but also bolt them and perhaps even bar our windows to give us a feeling of safety. Because we have lost control and respect for law and order, many Canadians feel that capital punishment is a deterrent to crime. 1 do believe that it is a deterrent, and many other Canadians do as well.
When we consider the type of society that we are building under fear, one would almost think we are living in the days of the Roman Empire, days in which the society destroyed itself from within. The Canadian people are losing much confidence in law makers. We are even destroying the practice of the shaking of the hand, which was probably a much better form of agreement reached between two people than that type of agreement made with lawyers. Even though agreements are carefully written, they are not as effective as the ones which were confirmed by a shake of the hand not so long ago.
As sophisticated, educated and experienced as we are, and with the knowledge gained from communications with other countries, we know full well that capital punishment is a deterrent. I have nothing against those who feel that capital punishment is not a deterrent. I think they have that right. I do believe in the democratic process, but I do not believe that the Government today is responding to the needs of the people. The Government is not listening. No wonder we are in the mess in this country that we are. We are in a mess economically, which is alarming. We are deteriorating slowly and creeping into a dictatorial system by which we have encouraged, by design or otherwise, the highjackings that are taking place, the hostage takings, and the sit-ins. As a result of the Hon. Member's beginning his speech with so many questions, I now ask myself whether he wants Government by Gallup poll. Is that what he wants? Does he think that Government should be a leader of public opinion or a follower?
That will be a big question in the next election. The people of Canada want their MPs to govern, not just follow. We could have another total debate on the Gallup poll. If I had more time, I would quote what Edmund Burke thought elected representatives should do, but I will leave that to my colleagues who want to enter this debate.
This Bill is different from any others which preceded it in that it specifies the type of capital punishment. Instead of hanging, I gather the Bill speaks about some kind of lethal injection. At first sight that might mean that the proposed execution would be more humane than in the past. However, I want to quote from an article published by Amnesty International on this very topic. It reads:
-it is a contradiction in terms to consider making the death penalty more humane-by, for instance, administering lethal drugs. Quite apart from the
question of a doctor having to defame the Hippocratic Oath and the recent Tokyo Declaration of the World Medical Association, such a discussion avoids the true hell of the death penalty. According to evidence from the United States, prisoners under sentence of death mutilate themselves, cover themselves in their own excrement, commit suicide or try to, and go insane-waiting, waiting to die. As Albert Camus wrote in his famous essay, Reflections on the Guillotine, in 1960: An execution, he wrote "is not simply death. It is just as different.. .as a concentration camp is from prison .... It adds to death a rule, a public premeditation known to the future victim ... for there to be an equivalence, the death penalty would have to punish a criminal who had warned the victim of the date at which he would inflict a horrible death on him and who, from that moment onward, had confined him at his mercy for months. Such a monster is not encountered in private life.
In other words, the method of execution is not that important. The inhumanity of a premeditated execution remains the same.
In 1976 Parliament debated at length the whole subject of capital punishment. At that time I voted freely for the abolition of capital punishment. 1 believe I said at that time that I had not always been an abolitionist.
When I was about 17 years of age, living in England, there was a tremendous series of murders. The police arrested a man by the name of John Evans. He was accused and eventually convicted of those horrible murders. In the public frenzy whipped up by the popular press at that time, 1 as a 16 or 17 year old was quite impressed. I thought "that guy deserves to die, he has to die." Then they killed him. He was executed. I had one little problem in the back of my mind. 1 repeat, I was an impressionable 16 or 17 years old. When reading the public accounts of the court proceedings, there was a problem that nagged me. It was that the man was illiterate. I thought to myself, how could an illiterate man understand the complexities of those proceedings. I had qualms. However, like most of the British population at that time, 1 welcomed his death sentence.
A few years after the man was dead and buried in whatever grave they buried criminals of that day, it became quite apparent that the man had been totally innocent. The man who was subsequently convicted of the crime was his landlord, a person by the name of Christie.
That incident was enough to change my view on capital punishment. It convinced me that for the rest of my life 1 would have to be extremely careful, not only in condemning people, but in destroying their ability to ever prove their innocence. Obviously there is nothing quicker than death to terminate one's possibilities of defending oneself.
Having turned into an abolitionist, frankly 1 do not believe that killing is always sinful. Sometimes it is absolutely necessary to protect your life or the lives of other people, such as in war. Then it can be necessary. However, I would do ail that I could in my power to prevent the outbreak of war. That is my personal opinion.
Does the state have the moral right in its responsibility to kill in order to protect its people? Perhaps that is the fundamental question raised by the Hon. Member for Calgary East. In the absence of any other way, probably yes, and probably if
November 19, 1982

the death of the aggressor were to be a deterrent. However, when we are speaking of the termination of human life, 1 cannot in honesty, intellect and conscience, accept the word "probably".
I do not need tremendous evidence, but certainly a preponderance of evidence, that the death penalty would be a deterrent. We do not have that evidence in Canada or throughout the world. 1 wish to quote the former solicitor general speaking in 1979 as follows:
-existing data indicates that there has been no disproportionate increase in the number of violent crimes.
1 can also quote Statistics Canada "Law Enforcement Statistics Section 1981 Preliminary Homicide Data", which 1 just received today. It reads:
Homicide and its constituent categories have generally been on the decline since 1977.
That is since the death penalty was abolished.
While homicide and murder rates for 1981 increased for the first time in four years, these rates still remain below those of 1977 and 1978.
To return again to the words of the former solicitor general, the Hon. Warren Allmand, he said:
-evidence shows that capital punishment does not effectively lower murder rates. In fact, the lowest murder rates in the world are found in those countries and those states where capital punishment has been abolished for a long time, as an example, Sweden, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Rhode Island, Maine. Conversely, those that have retained capital punishment over a long period have the highest murder rate, as an example, France, Spain, Florida, South Carolina, Louisiana and Georgia.
No one has been able to prove that capital punishment is a deterrent and even if there were evidence to support that theory, only a preponderance of that evidence will convince. 1 will come back again to Amnesty International. Speaking at the Conference on the Abolition of the Death Penalty, Declaration of Stockholm, December 11, 1977, this Conference on the abolition of the death penalty, composed of more than 200 delegates and participants from Africa, Asia, Europe, the Middle East, North and South America and the Caribbean region, recalled that the death penalty is the ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment and violates the right to life. The Declaration says, among other things, that execution is an act of violence, and violence tends to provoke violence; the death penalty has never been shown to have a special deterrent effect; execution is irrevocable and can be inflicted on the innocent.
I have already cited a case in point which happened in England during the time 1 was living there. There was another case, the name of which escapes me now, but it was quite recent. It took place, 1 believe, in the eastern part of Canada, where a man was proven innocent after many years of imprisonment. These cases do happen, and in my judgment, Mr. Speaker, we cannot, as a society, afford to condone even one case of the innocent being punished.
Finally, the Hon. Member spoke of the social ills of our time. I felt he spoke with some nostalgia for the past, but nostalgia, like many other things, is not always too accurate. He spoke of the "good old days". He spoke of the Roman Empire. I can think of little less brutality than that which was
Capital Punishment
shown to the world at the time of the Roman Empire. He spoke of prostitution. Is that something new? He spoke of other crimes, but he did not speak of the undercurrent, the underlying reasons for the rise in social crimes, and there are many, not least of which, perhaps, is the unequal distribution of wealth and opportunity for Canadians. But we can rectify that, and this Government does intend to rectify it. However, you do not create a better society by killing half its members.

Mr. Speaker,
1 would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kushner) for introducing this Bill today. He is speaking up on behalf of the Canadian people. He understands the role of a Member of Parliament and that of a politician, and he made his point very well. We are the servants of the people, but there are so many in this House who have reversed that over the last few years. Now it is the people who are the servants, and somehow the Liberals think they are the masters and they will keep the people in line.
1 believe that capital punishment should be in our Criminal Code. It should be there when needed. It is not necessary, in my opinion, that we have capital punishment for every type of murder, but it should be there. The United States is returning to capital punishment in many of its States.
The former speaker from the Liberal Party mentioned the problems of society today, but it is the Liberals who have introduced the permissive society into this country, easy bail and weekend passes, and what have you, and if we did return to the "good old days", as the Hon. Member from Calgary mentioned, we could bring back the paddle and the strap and have some discipline. That is what the criminals fear. We would not have so much crime today if criminals knew they were going to be faced with these punishments.
The group who really understands crime and murderers, Mr. Speaker, is the police. The Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police have made their point repeatedly in calling for the return of capital punishment, and they are far better judges than we are in respect of whether or not capital punishment should be returned. Police are not irresponsible people, they have experience in dealing with crime and criminals and we should be listening to their advice, but we completely ignore it. We will not back them up, and this is a serious mistake we have been making.
The criminal element, the underworld, does not want capital punishment brought back. We saw a recent example of that in St. Calixte, Quebec. This is a story out of the Winnipeg Free Press dated November 18, 1982, where threats and shots failed to halt a capital punishment crusade, and I quote:
Undaunted by threatening phone calls and an apparent attempt on his life last week, the head of a group lobbying for the return of capital punishment says he will press on with his campaign.
Fernand Pellerin, president and director general of the Citizens Committee of Canada, said he was driving near this town 40 kilometres north of Montreal last Thursday when a man in a car travelling in the opposite direction fired two shotgun blasts at him.
The first blast blew out the windshield, the second, the rear window. This man established the Citizens' Committee last

November 19, 1982
Capital Punishment
December, Mr. Speaker, and the committee is currently organizing across Canada to demand a referendum on capital punishment. It would seem that the underworld will go to any limits to deal with anyone who is organizing to this extent.
There was a very sad case earlier this year that touched me very deeply. During the Archambault prison riot last spring or early summer, a prison guard was knifed to death, murdered, and left to die in a pool of his own blood. In some dark hall in the prison, I suppose. The prison guard was knifed to death by a convicted murderer, and the sad thing here, Mr. Speaker, is he had only one hour to go on his shift, and not only did he have one hour to go on his shift, but he was to retire in one hour. He was 60 years of age and he was knifed to death in a prison by convicted murderers. That was his fate because we will not re-introduce capital punishment.
The Liberal Member who spoke prior to me mentioned that some innocent people have been put away. That has happened in some cases and that is most unfortunate, but there are many cases where a murderer has murdered twice. In Winnipeg, where I come from, there have been cases where an individual has murdered twice. I recall one case where a murderer was imprisoned for eight years, he was released, and within a short period of time murdered again. He murdered a young girl at the same hotel where he had committed his first murder. This should prove that there are a lot of advantages in having capital punishment.
The Hon. Member for Calgary East mentioned the lastest opinion poll where five out of every six Canadians favour the suggestion that a referendum be held. I have no objection to having a referendum. I would like to see the next Conservative Government have a legitimate free vote again, a proper debate on capital punishment, referring the subject matter to committee, because the type of capital punishment we use has been mentioned. We can discuss the rope and other ways that capital punishment can be implemented. We could also have police officers as witnesses, or anyone else. I am not afraid to have a proper debate on capital punishment. We would certainly be acting on behalf of the majority.
We continually read, Mr. Speaker, of the horror stories. There is the recent case of a man admitting in court that he killed 30 people. He was not mentally disturbed, he was a hit man and had murdered 30 people. Then down in Atlanta, Georgia, there was the slaying of 38 women, described as Atlanta's hidden tragedy. Think of the 38 families and the suffering they have gone through. I hear repeatedly these arguments from the Liberals, but they never mention anything about the families or the victims, they are always so concerned about the murderer. They would not want anything to happen to the murderer. There is never a word at all about the mother or the father or the daughter or anyone else. Another horror story is that of a nun who was raped and robbed. A lot of the murderers are not just satisfied with murdering an individual, they want to rape and murder them. Heaven only knows what else happens before the final thrust, Mr. Speaker. A colleague
of mine, the Hon. Member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), recently distributed a questionnaire on capital punishment, and 2,223 of the people responding indicated they favour capital punishment, with 112 favoring abolition. So in some areas of the country 90 per cent of Canadians want the return of capital punishment.
I remember a very sad case in Toronto a couple of years ago of three grown up men sexually attacking a 14 year old shoeshine boy who had been working on Yonge Street. They picked him up and took him away to some deserted building and sexually tortured him before they killed him. Heaven only knows what that 14 year old lad went through at the hands of those three men. As I remember, some of them, when they were convicted, said they would sooner receive capital punishment than be sent to jail. Then there is another case in Chicago of one man murdering 36 people, and he was not mentally unbalanced. On and on it goes, Mr. Speaker.
I feel it is about time we started listening to the Canadian people. It would not be a bad idea for this Bill to be referred to committee. The Liberal Member who spoke prior to me made some excellent suggestions, and the place to discuss them is in committee with witnesses. Because this Bill is sent to committee does not mean that we would immediately start hanging people. Perhaps when we have finished our deliberations we would find that we would not have to implement capital punishment but that there might have to be some changes made in the law.
I do not want to be the one who is going to come anywhere close to talking out this Bill, and I hope the next Liberal to speak on this Bill will consider allowing it to go to committee.

Mr. Speaker, since four o'clock I have listened to this debate with some interest, particularly to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kushner) and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine ((Mr. McKenzie). As I listened to the Hon. Member for Calgary East and heard him go through a litany of what was wrong with this country, such as bilingualism, the metric system, the Post Office, highjackings and hostage takings, and heard him try to put the issue of capital punishment in that context, I could not help but think he is a man who yearns for simple answers to complex problems. He is a man who thinks that the good old days, where questions and answers were simple, where everyone knew what was right and what was wrong and where appropriate punishments were always applicable, is an age that he would like to return to. I suggest that that time never existed, and certainly to return to it in respect of capital punishment would be a regressive and barbaric move. I can understand his emotions. We all share in the anguish of the victims of violent crime.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine mentioned the tragic incidents at Archambeault Penitentiary. The guard that he referred to is a constituent of mine, and it was and is a tragic situation. The Hon. Member also spoke of victims of crime, that somehow those of us who are abolitionists have no feelings for them. That, I suggest, is foolishness. Does the Hon. Member suggest for one minute that somehow capital punish-
November 19, 1982

ment will recompense the victims of crime, the families of those who are murdered? That is not going to bring them back from the dead.
We live in a complex society today, Mr. Speaker, and there are always those who think we can return to simpler times. I refer to a debate in this House on June 11, 1981, when my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), made the following remarks:
People feel that the moral order has been transgressed, as it has, and that something must be done to show that these are not mundane events but rather events which, if permitted or regarded lightly, would eventually call into question the very basis of civilized society. They are morally outraged that such things can happen. It is moral outrage we are dealing with when we talk about the call for a return to capital punishment, moral outrage and powerlessness.
That is a very human emotion. When we have this call for a return to capital punishment it gives us a sense that we are restoring the balance, making things equal. It satisfies an emotional need; an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth. But at what price, Mr. Speaker?
My colleague, the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni), referred to the Evans-Christie case of a number of years ago in Great Britain, where an innocent man was hanged. She also made passing reference to a case in Nova Scotia recently, that of Donald Marshall, who at the ripe old age of 17 was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder. Now it apears, Mr. Speaker, that Donald Marshall is innocent. Suppose he had been hanged by the neck until dead? What would we do today? Would we somehow restore him to life and say, sorry, young man, we made a mistake? The Hon. Member for York South-Weston made reference to the fact that justice is not always done in these matters. The case of Donald Marshall is a case in point. 1 should like to refer to a story which appeared in The Globe and Mail with reference to the atmosphere at his trial. The headline read, "Racial tensions, fear gripped Micmac's trial". Of course, Marshall is a Micmac Indian, and in that atmosphere of racial tension and fear, he was convicted on the flimsiest of circumstantial evidence.
Apropos of such cases, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine said that it was most unfortunate that an innocent man or woman spent 11 years of his or her life in jail or was executed. Indeed it is very unfortunate, especially if one is dead.
Is our system of justice equal? I suggest that Hon. Members opposite should check the figures for American prisons to see how many Blacks are in American jails in proportion to their presence in the American population. How many are in jail? Far in excess of the ratio in Canada. How many native people are in Canadian prisons in proportion to their presence in the population? How many poor people are in Canadian prisons, people without power, money or connections? Who gets convicted in the end? Does the system of justice in Canada apply fairly? Can we guarantee that the innocent will not be executed?
Capital Punishment
There are some interesting figures and comments made with regard to capital punishment by those who have been involved in it. I refer the House to some remarks made by Albert Pierrepoint who, for over 25 years, was the British hangman. He officiated at several hundred hangings. In 1974, years after his retirement, he wrote his discreet memoirs. The memoirs include the following passage:
Executions solve nothing and are only an antiquated relic of a primitive desire for revenge which takes the easy way out and hands the responsibility for revenge to other people ... It is said to be a deterrent. I cannot agree. There have been murders since the beginning of time and we shall go on looking for deterrents until the end of time. If death were a deterrent, I might be expected to know. It is I who faced them last, young lads and girls, working men and grandmothers, I have been amazed to see the courage with which they take that walk into the unknown ... All the men and women whom I have faced at that final moment convince me that in what I have done I have not prevented a single murder.
There are some interesting statistics. In the 1950s a Canadian joint parliamentary committee caused a tabulation to be made on the only matter on which full data was available- persons sentenced to death in Canada from Confederation onward. That tabulation was carried forward in "Capital Punishment" published by the Department of Justice in 1965. It indicates that from Confederation in 1867 to 1962, 1,487 people were sentenced to death in Canada. Of this number only 47.7 per cent were executed, 38.4 per cent had their sentences commuted, and 13.9 per cent were otherwise dealt with by courts of appeal. Thus, for the 95 years that we had the death penalty in Canada, if the police solved the case, and the murderer was convicted, that murderer still had a better than even chance of not being executed. It is striking that the British figures for commutation in this century are quite similar to the Canadian experience. Even if all the proper procedures are followed, there is no certainty.
As far as Gallup polls or other polls are concerned as to what Canadian people or people in general want, there have been suggestions that those of us who are abolitionists are not following the will of the people. I would say two things. First, polls are an imperfect instrument of measurement. I draw to the attention of the Hon. Member for Calgary East, the sponsor of the Bill, that the Harris poll taken in the United States in June 1973 began by asking respondents whether or not they believed in capital punishment. Three out of five said yes, but then the poll went on to ask a more complex set of follow-up questions, suggesting capital punishment as a penalty for a specific list of crimes. For none of those specific crimes did more than 41 per cent favour the death penalty; a drop of 20 per cent when one moved from the general and abstract to the specific and concrete. Certainly when one asks a general question one gets a general answer, but when one zeros in on more specific questions, the picture changes-the polls change and the response is different.
If, as the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine suggested, we are not doing our duty as Members of Parliament and reflecting the will of the people on this issue, is that our job? Sure it is, partially, but it is also our job to think. It is also our job to look at the facts dispassionately and render a decision

November 19, 1982
Capital Punishment
based upon the facts. It is also our job to be compassionate and progressive.
I remind the Hon. Member for Calgary East of Edmund Burke in his now classic 1774 "Address to the Electors of Bristol" who said that a representative owed his constituents:
-his unbiased opinion, his mature judgment, his enlightened conscience... Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment; and he betrays, instead of serving you, if he sacrifices it to your opinion.
If we were only to be robots reflecting the opinions of the electorate, then we are not needed because the opinions of the
electorate in this technological age can be simply transmitted by pushing a button.
